subject: astronomy
intro: Astronomy points to the observatory, the spacecraft design office and the lecture hall — people who observe the sky, interpret starlight and engineer the machines that travel there.

roles.title: Astronomers
roles.what: Observe, research and interpret astronomical phenomena — planets, stars, galaxies and the universe's expansion — to increase basic knowledge or apply it to practical problems.
roles.where: Topics 13 to 16 — starlight and magnitude, stellar evolution, the Milky Way, redshift and cosmology, dark matter and dark energy — are precisely the observing and interpreting work astronomers do.

roles.title: Physicists
roles.what: Conduct research into physical phenomena and develop theories from observation and experiment — the discipline behind explaining gravity, radiation, stellar interiors and the universe at large.
roles.where: Planetary motion and gravity (topic 8) — Kepler's third law, stable orbits, Newton's universal gravitation — and the radiation and distance-modulus topics of 13 are physics applied to the sky.

roles.title: Aerospace Engineers
roles.what: Design, construct and test aircraft, missiles and spacecraft, evaluating how materials and equipment stand up to flight conditions and recommending improvements in designs and testing techniques.
roles.where: Spacecraft trajectories to the Moon (topic 9.4), Kepler's third law and stable orbits (topic 8), and telescope objectives, aperture and resolution (topic 11) give the orbital-mechanics and hardware grounding.

roles.title: Atmospheric, Earth, Marine, and Space Sciences Teachers, Postsecondary
roles.what: Teach university courses in the physical sciences beyond chemistry and physics — astronomy, planetary science and Earth science — often combining teaching with research on their own observing programmes.
roles.where: The specification's arc from Planet Earth through the Solar System to cosmology (topics 1 to 16) matches the introductory university astronomy and Earth-science courses such teachers deliver.
